blocks.text: V. There remains the fifth question, concerning the punishment that God inflicted on the Jews who ate the quails. The sin was this: weary of their condition, they had murmured against God as follows: Who will give us meat to eat! We remember the fish that we ate in Egypt for nothing, and the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic: but now our soul is dried up, and nothing is before our eyes except the Manna, Num. XI, 4. 5. 6. Hence the Psalmist, Ps. LXXVIII, 19: Speaking against God they said, Can God furnish a table in this wilderness? Behold! he struck the rock so that waters flowed and streams overflowed. Can he also give food? Will he provide meat for his people? In these words, 1. they show themselves remarkably ungrateful, since they prefer their former condition, that is, the Egyptian servitude, from which God had rescued them with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, to the liberty they now enjoyed. Who, hearing this, would not have thought that they had lived sumptuously in Egypt and in great prosperity? Yet there they had lived wretchedly, pressed and nearly crushed under Pharaoh's yoke. But it is customary for the ungrateful, even when raised to greater things, to extol the past and disdain [II, 674] the present, lest they acknowledge that they owe thanks to anyone for the improvement of their state. 2. They reveal a remarkable ἀῤῥωστίαν τῆς διανοίας [arrhōstian tēs dianoias] in that they prefer little fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic, in short carnal things, to spiritual goods and to the glorious presence of God, which he had attested by so many signs and miracles. 3. Not content with the Manna, from which the necessary sustenance was abundantly supplied to them, they had demanded meat besides, and had limited God, as it says in Psal. LXXVIII, 41., that is, they had defined his power by their own judgement, asking not only to be delivered, but to be delivered in this or that way. 4. After having experienced God's power so many times, these are nevertheless words of distrust: Can God furnish a table in this wilderness? Can he also give food? God therefore, justly provoked to anger, promises that he will give meat, not only for one or two days but for a whole month, so that, having eaten it not only to satiety but even to nausea and loathing, they would at last spit it out and reject it. These are the words of one whose mind is stirred, and who had heard the people's prayers only in his anger. So when the month was over, while they still had in their mouths the food with which they had gorged themselves, God, blazing against them, struck the people with a great plague. Aben Ezra takes this to be pestilence. There are some who infer from Psal. CVI, 15. that רזון, that is, leanness or consumption, is meant. Others explain it otherwise. But I side with those for whom this plague is fire, by which some of this people were consumed. For so David has it, Psal. LXXVIII, [col. 109] 21: Therefore the Lord heard and was enraged (hearing, that is, what is reported in the preceding verse, Can God furnish a table, etc.) and a fire was kindled in Jacob. Understand the fire spoken of in Num. XI, 1: And when the people complained, it was evil in the ears of the Lord. So the Lord heard and was enraged, and the fire of the Lord, blazing up, consumed the outermost parts of the camp, etc., up to the fourth verse, where the things that are afterwards explained more fully in the rest of the chapter seem to be narrated briefly by πρόληψιν [prolēpsin]. And the same place was given a double name: one, Tabera, from the burning, Num. XI, 3.; the other, Kibrot-taava, because those who had craved meat were buried there, Num. XI, 34. ^{(15)}. There is also another example of similar obstinacy in this same people.

[II, 675] For in Exod. XVI, 2. we read that the congregation murmured and said to Moses and Aaron: Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to the full! But you have brought us into this wilderness, so that this whole assembly may be destroyed by hunger. But in what seems a like case, the judgement was unlike. For to these murmurers God granted quails that very evening and Manna the next day, exacting no punishment from them, Exod. XVI, 12. 13. Indeed, God can either punish the same sins in justice or pardon and remit them in mercy. Yet many reasons can be given why he punished the latter severely for what he had kindly remitted to the former. First, if anyone falls again into sins which God has once remitted, he sins more gravely, because besides God's justice he also spurns his mercy, and so he is evil because God was good. Moreover, the former had murmured because they were pressed by hunger and the want of everything. But the latter had Manna for food, which satisfied them, so that their so greedily desiring meat and demanding it so importunately was a cry wrung not by necessity but by wicked lust. Finally, the former were still untaught, and the Law had not yet been given, immediately after the departure from Egypt; the latter murmur when already instructed, and after receiving the Law, so that the sin is graver. So it is not surprising that God, who had spared the former, dealt so severely with these.
